state_background_check.value: Ambiguous — New Mexico has two felony-disqualification provisions with inconsistent scope. NMSA 1978 §10-1-2 broadly bars anyone convicted of a 'felonious or infamous crime' (absent a pardon or restoration of political rights) from being 'elected or appointed to any public office in this state,' language broad enough on its face to arguably reach federal offices held by NM residents. But the companion restoration statute, NMSA 1978 §31-13-1 ('Felony conviction; restoration of right to hold office of public trust'), frames the same bar narrowly as applying only to 'an office of public trust for the state, a county, a municipality or a district' — omitting federal office. Even under the broadest reading of §10-1-2, any state-imposed qualification for Congress beyond the U.S. Constitution's own textual qualifications would likely be preempted under U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton (1995). No New Mexico court decision was found squarely resolving whether §10-1-2 reaches congressional candidacy specifically, so genuine ambiguity remains.
state_background_check.snippet: no person convicted of a felonious or infamous crime, unless such person has been pardoned or restored to political rights, shall be qualified to be elected or appointed to any public office in this state

platform.value: Supports expanding affordable housing, prioritizing mental health and substance abuse treatment for individuals experiencing chronic homelessness, strengthening veteran housing programs and targeted assistance for vulnerable populations, strengthening workforce development, improving government accountability in homelessness programs, and promoting community-based solutions.
platform.snippet: My Plan to Address Homelessness Expand Affordable Housing I will support policies that increase the supply of affordable housing, reduce unnecessary regulatory barriers, and encourage public-private partnerships to create more housing opportunities for working families, seniors, veterans, and individuals experiencing homelessness. Prioritize Mental Health and Substance Abuse Treatment Many individuals experiencing chronic homelessness struggle with mental health challenges or substance use disorders. I support expanding access to treatment, recovery programs, crisis intervention services, and long-term behavioral health care. Support Veterans and Vulnerable Populations No veteran who served our nation should be left without a home. I will advocate for stronger veteran housing programs and targeted assistance for seniors, individuals with disabilities, youth aging out of foster care, and survivors of domestic violence. Strengthen Workforce Development Stable employment is one of the strongest pathways out of homelessness. I support job training programs, workforce development initiatives, apprenticeships, and partnerships with local businesses that help individuals gain skills and achieve long-term self-sufficiency. Improve Government Accountability Taxpayer dollars must produce measurable results. I will push for greater transparency, performance standards, and outcome-based funding to ensure homelessness programs effectively move people from the streets into stable housing and permanent employment. Promote Community-Based Solutions Local communities often understand their challenges best. I support empowering cities, counties, nonprofits, faith-based organizations, and community leaders to develop innovative solutions tailored to their unique needs.

platform.value: Supports increasing the mental health workforce, expanding telehealth services, reducing barriers to care, improving access in rural and underserved communities, expanding access to treatment programs and recovery services including medication-assisted treatment, and investing in prevention programs and early intervention.
platform.snippet: My Plan for Mental Health and Addiction Recovery Expand Access to Mental Health Care Every American should have timely access to quality mental health services regardless of income or location. I support increasing the mental health workforce, expanding telehealth services, reducing barriers to care, and improving access in rural and underserved communities. Combat the Addiction Crisis Addiction is a public health challenge that requires evidence-based solutions. I will support expanded access to treatment programs, recovery services, medication-assisted treatment, and community-based support systems that help individuals achieve long-term recovery. Invest in Prevention and Early Intervention The best way to address mental illness and addiction is before a crisis occurs. I support increased funding for prevention programs, school-based mental health services, community outreach initiatives, and early intervention resources

bio_summary.value: Ben Ray Luján ( / l uː ˈ h ɑː n / loo- HAHN ; [ 1 ] born June 7, 1972) is an American politician serving since 2021 as the junior United States senator from New Mexico . From 2009 to 2021, he represented New Mexico's 3rd congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives ; he served as assistant speaker [ a ] from 2019 to 2021. Luján is a self-described progressive Democrat. [ 2 ] Before being elected to Congress, Luján served as a member of the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission from 2005 to 2008, where he was also chairman. [ 3 ] He and Senator Martin Heinrich are the co-deans of New Mexico's congressional delegation . Luján served as chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee from 2014 to 2019; Democrats won a House majority in the 2018 elections . [ 4 ]
